title: I built a mobile co-op rafting game with AI, but the hard part was making two browsers agree on one boat
author: CompetitiveSyrup4704
selftext:
I’ve been building Chattoplay and the games on it by myself, using AI throughout the development process.

this is RIPTIDE DUO. two players share one raft and each person controls one paddle. you can invite a friend or use online matchmaking if you join alone.

AI helped me turn the initial idea into working code, but it wasn’t a one-prompt game. most of the work ended up being an iteration loop: build something, run it in two browsers, find where the clients disagree, fix it, and play it again.

the game is a self-contained Three.js project. the river follows a seeded spline, and the water, cliffs, trees, foam and other parts of the scene are generated in code rather than assembled from a downloaded level.

for multiplayer, one player owns the boat simulation. paddle strokes are sent as events, while the other player receives boat snapshots and interpolates between them. I used AI to help implement and test that system, especially things like late joins, disconnects, duplicate inputs, checkpoint recovery and mobile camera framing.

the short clip is from the current build.

you can play it here:

[https://chattoplay.com/play/riptide-duo?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=community&utm\_campaign=riptide\_duo\_launch\_202608&utm\_content=r\_aigamedev\_devlog](https://chattoplay.com/play/riptide-duo?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=riptide_duo_launch_202608&utm_content=r_aigamedev_devlog)

I’m curious where AI has been most useful for other solo developers after the first prototype works. for me, the repeated test-and-fix loop has been more valuable than the initial code generation.
